record.paper_title: Answering open questions in biology using spatial genomics and structured methods
record.original_question: How does the three-dimensional spatial organization of the genome inside intact cells affect transcription, specifically at the boundaries between active A compartments and inactive B compartments, and what spatial features distinguish different genomic compartments beyond the A/B partition?

evidence.quote: Although chromatin conformation capture methods such as Hi-C are able to capture these compartments [28, 29], the link between these compartments and their transcription products is still being uncovered on a spatial level within intact cells. What occurs on the border between A and B compartments? Are there features that further distinguish different genomic compartments?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Inside an intact eukaryotic cell, the genome is spatially organized in three dimensions and can be partitioned, on the basis of chromatin conformation capture data, into two broad classes of regions called the A compartment (associated with transcriptionally active, open chromatin) and the B compartment (associated with transcriptionally inactive, closed chromatin). Investigate the following:

(a) Characterize, in a spatially resolved manner within intact cells, how the three-dimensional arrangement of chromatin influences transcriptional activity. In particular, describe quantitatively what happens to nascent transcription, RNA localization, and chromatin state at the interfaces (borders) between A and B compartments.

(b) Determine whether there exist additional, finer spatial or structural features—beyond the binary A/B partition—that further distinguish distinct genomic compartments from one another (for example, sub-compartments, contact-frequency signatures, radial positioning, or association with nuclear bodies), and provide criteria that rigorously identify such features.

Provide a framework (experimental, computational, or mathematical) capable of answering (a) and (b) and validate it on genome-wide data from intact cells.
artifact.status_search_result: The question concerns an active area of research in spatial genomics. While sub-compartments (e.g., A1/A2/B1/B2/B3) have been identified via Hi-C and finer-resolution methods, and recent imaging/spatial transcriptomics work has begun probing A/B boundaries, a comprehensive spatially resolved characterization of transcription at A/B compartment borders and a definitive enumeration of additional distinguishing features remain unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Sub-compartments identified by Hi-C (Rao et al.)
status_evidence.snippet: Identifies six sub-compartments (A1, A2, B1, B2, B3, B4) beyond the A/B partition, indicating finer structural distinctions exist but their full functional characterization is ongoing.
status_evidence.claim: Sub-compartments beyond A/B have been identified, but their complete spatial/functional distinctions remain under investigation.
